title: Buy, Wait or Run It Longer: U.S. Tractor Replacement Decisions Before EPA 2027
summary: GHG Phase 3 is repealed, the 2027 NOx rule is still unfinished and used sleepers cost more. How fleets, brokers and hybrids should time tractor replacement.
body_markdown:
The replacement plan you approved in the spring assumed three things: the 2027 rules would be settled by now, used tractors would be cheap to buy and easy to sell, and you could order on your usual calendar. None of that held up. The model year 2026 build slots most fleets wanted are gone. The final 2027 rule has not been published. And your oldest tractors, the ones the plan said to trade this quarter, are now worth more on trade than they were a year ago while costing more to keep running.


The question for an asset fleet or hybrid operator this week: do you order 2027 tractors before pricing is final, wait for the rule, run current units longer, or move more freight to owner-operators and brokered capacity? Each answer is right for some units. The mistake is picking one for the whole fleet.


## Where the rules actually stand


Half of the 2027 regulatory cliff is gone. The other half is still moving.


**GHG Phase 3 is repealed.** On February 12, 2026, EPA finalized the rescission of the 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding and repealed all motor vehicle GHG standards, including the Phase 3 heavy-duty standards for model year 2027 and later. The final rule, published February 18, took effect April 20, 2026. EPA says manufacturers no longer have any future obligation to measure, control or report GHG emissions for highway engines and vehicles. Litigation continues. In an October 5, 2026 order in *American Public Health Association v. EPA* , the D.C. Circuit denied a motion to stay the rescission, refused to put the consolidated cases on hold, and gave the parties 30 days to propose a briefing format. For the 2027 buying cycle, plan as though no federal tractor GHG standard applies.


**The 2027 NOx standard still stands, but its cost is unsettled.** EPA's December 2022 rule, published in January 2023, sets a 0.035 g/hp-hr NOx limit under normal operation starting with model year 2027. On July 14, 2026, EPA proposed amendments that would keep model year 2026 emission warranty periods for 2027 and later engines, delay the longer useful-life requirements to model year 2030, allow nonconformance penalties (NCPs) for medium and heavy heavy-duty engines beginning in model year 2027, and replace DEF-related derates and speed limits on new engines with audible or visual warnings. Comments closed August 29, 2026. As of this week, EPA's own rule page still lists it as a proposal. Trade press on October 24 reported that the final rule is expected by year end.


The dollar figures in the proposal set the bounds of your price risk. EPA estimates up to $6,000 in warranty savings per new diesel truck and net savings of up to $12 billion. Under the proposed first-year NCP schedule, a heavy heavy-duty engine family certified at 100 mg/hp-hr would pay $5,875 per engine. At 45 mg/hp-hr it would pay $904. Whether that reaches your invoice is up to the manufacturer. In late-October trade reporting, several said they will sell current-emission engines alongside fully compliant 0.035 engines into 2027. Others plan to rely on emission credits, and at least one compliant engine is not expected on vehicles until May.


**California is in court, not in your order spec.** Congressional Review Act resolutions signed June 12, 2025 overturned the waivers for California's Advanced Clean Trucks and heavy-duty Omnibus rules, and CARB says those resolutions are being challenged. CARB has withdrawn its waiver request for Advanced Clean Fleets and is not enforcing the waiver-dependent high-priority and drayage fleet provisions. On October 31, 2025, a federal court in the Eastern District of California preliminarily barred CARB from enforcing the Clean Truck Partnership with truck makers. A June 2026 legal summary said cross-motions for summary judgment were set for an August 2026 hearing, with a merits ruling possible in late 2026 or early 2027. California lanes need watching; a national order should not hinge on it.


**Tariffs are part of the equipment price now.** Proclamation 10984, issued October 17, 2025, put a 25% Section 232 duty on imported medium and heavy-duty trucks and key parts, including engines, transmissions, tires and chassis, starting November 1, 2025. For USMCA-qualifying trucks, the duty applies only to non-U.S. content. The Commerce Department's February 2, 2026 procedures make those content determinations valid for one calendar year, and importers had to file for 2027 models by October 1, 2026. Parts and tires hit maintenance cost per mile, not just sticker price.


## What the order and resale data say


Preliminary Class 8 order figures for September 2026, the first month of model year 2027 ordering, depend on which monthly report you read. One put North American net orders at 21,300 units, up 3% year over year, with 263,499 orders year to date (up 95%). It said the 2027 NOx pre-buy has ended and surcharge-free model year 2026 build slots are effectively sold out. Another put preliminary orders at 18,700, down 9.5%, and its final count at 19,172, down 7%. Both pointed to an unfinished rule, unknown pricing and the uneven opening of 2027 order boards. U.S. trailer orders in the same month reached 43,059 units, up 385% year over year in one industry tally. Many fleets are refreshing trailers now and postponing the tractor decision.


Resale is where the math changed. A used-truck valuation guide for September 2026 had average retail prices for used sleepers down 0.5% from August but up 9.9% year over year. Auction prices were up 24.8% and wholesale up 5.2%. One marketplace's September data showed used day cab and sleeper inventory down 36.03% year over year. A separate price guide put average September values at $92,330 for two-year-old sleepers, $54,340 for five-year-olds and $25,500 for ten-year-olds. The valuation guide expects more three- to five-year-old sleepers to come back on trade as new-truck deliveries catch up, though high capacity utilization should limit the effect on values.


On the cost side, an industry research institute's 2026 operational-cost analysis found that 2025 repair and maintenance rose 8.6% to $0.215 per mile, excluding tires and towing, as average truck age, trade cycles and annual miles all increased. Respondents' average tractor trade cycle was 7.0 years and 633,772 miles, with 85,991 miles per truck per year. Fleets with fewer than five trucks had the highest truckload R&M costs, and the report ties that directly to lower spending on equipment: "fleets that spend less on asset procurement typically must spend more to maintain them."


## Where margin breaks


Extending a trade cycle is cheap until it isn't. The costs that hit at once are the ones that sink a hold strategy:


-


**R&M cost per mile by unit, not fleet average.** A healthy fleet average can hide a group of high-mileage units running well above it until one bad quarter exposes them.


-


**Downtime as lost revenue.** A tractor in the shop for nine days means lost loads, an idle driver who may quit, and a commitment you cover with brokered capacity at spot rates or miss.


-


**Residual timing.** Today's used-tractor values reward selling sooner. If more three- to five-year-old units come back on trade as deliveries arrive, the sellers who wait may get lower prices.


-


**Pricing you cannot lock.** Model year 2027 orders are going in before the final rule. Whether an NCP, a warranty change or a tariff line ends up in your invoice depends on contract language you should read before you sign.


## The decision by business model


**Asset carriers.** Treat replacement as a decision about specific tractors, not the whole fleet. Rank units by trailing 12-month R&M per mile, unscheduled downtime days, and mileage relative to your own replacement point. Sell the worst tail into today's resale market. Order a smaller 2027 tranche to learn the new aftertreatment on your own lanes before committing the bulk. Get written answers on whether the engine is current-emission or 0.035, whether an NCP or surcharge can be added after the order, and what emission warranty term applies if the final rule changes it.


**Freight brokers.** You own no tractors, but you buy the results of carriers' equipment decisions: older fleets mean more breakdowns and recovery loads. Owner-operator economics were already tight: the same cost analysis put 2025 carrier-contracted owner-operator rates at $2.08 per mile against a $2.21 truckload marginal cost. Watch on-time and breakdown-related fall-off by carrier, and price recovery coverage into your committed lanes instead of absorbing it.


**Hybrids.** The real choice is the asset-to-brokered mix. Every tractor you don't replace becomes a lane you broker at whatever the market charges that week. Decide which freight must stay on your trucks (dedicated, high-service) and size replacement to that, not the old fleet total.


## Encoding the replacement decision


A Southeast reefer fleet, a regional flatbed operation and a retail-dedicated hybrid each have a different replacement threshold. Serious shops encode theirs in the system instead of a yearly spreadsheet:


-


**Equipment fields that drive decisions:** engine family and emission spec, in-service date, warranty expiration, and lifetime and trailing R&M per mile on each unit record.


-


**Statuses for the in-between:** "replacement candidate," "on order," and "pending sale," so planning stops long-haul assignments before a sale.


-


**Cost-per-mile visibility by unit and lane:** maintenance, downtime and fuel allocated to the unit, not hidden in overhead.


-


**Capacity rules that follow the plan:** when an asset is pulled, its committed lanes route automatically to approved carrier pools at a pre-set rate ceiling.


-


**Permissions on spend:** repairs above a set percentage of the unit's residual value need approval, so no one rebuilds an engine in a truck you plan to sell next month.


## Before you sign a 2027 order


1.


Pull 12 months of R&M per mile and downtime days by tractor. Rank the bottom quintile.


2.


Get current trade and auction values for those units, and decide which to sell now.


3.


Get engine spec, NCP or surcharge pass-through, warranty and tariff terms in writing.


4.


Assume no federal GHG tractor standard for 2027; watch the NOx final rule.


5.


Map which lanes go to brokered or owner-operator capacity, and at what cost.


## FAQ


### Are the EPA GHG Phase 3 truck standards still in effect for 2027?


No. EPA repealed all motor vehicle GHG standards, including heavy-duty Phase 3, in a final rule dated February 12, 2026 that took effect April 20, 2026. The D.C. Circuit denied a stay on October 5, 2026.


### Is the EPA 2027 heavy-duty NOx standard still happening?


Yes. The 0.035 g/hp-hr standard from the 2023 rule still applies starting with model year 2027. EPA's July 14, 2026 proposal would keep current warranty periods, delay longer useful-life requirements to model year 2030, and allow nonconformance penalties, but it had not been finalized as of late October 2026.


### What would a nonconformance penalty add to a 2027 tractor?


Under EPA's proposed first-year schedule, a heavy heavy-duty engine family certified at 100 mg/hp-hr would pay $5,875 per engine, and one at 45 mg/hp-hr would pay $904. Whether the manufacturer passes that through depends on your purchase terms.


### Is there still a pre-buy window for model year 2026 tractors?


Effectively no. Monthly industry order reports for September 2026 said the 2027 NOx pre-buy has ended and surcharge-free model year 2026 build slots are effectively sold out.


### Should a fleet extend its trade cycle in 2027?


Only unit by unit. Industry cost data shows R&M rising to $0.215 per mile in 2025 as trade cycles lengthened, while September 2026 used-sleeper values were up 9.9% year over year at retail. The worst units are often worth more sold now than kept.


### Do Section 232 tariffs affect tractor and parts costs?


Yes. Since November 1, 2025, a 25% duty has applied to imported medium and heavy-duty trucks and key parts such as engines, transmissions and tires. USMCA-qualifying trucks pay only on non-U.S. content, under annual Commerce Department determinations.
